sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

<project_instructions path="/private/var/folders/24/2ff01nsx7cs9005l3jbptw8c0000gp/T/shallot-eval-color-on-key-Rqp8as/app/AGENTS.md">
# Shallot project

Explore this project's entry, plugins and checks first; reuse its setup.

- Learn the API from the installed package, not memory. `bunx shallot create --help` lists the examples in `node_modules/@dylanebert/shallot/examples/`; start from the nearest one, its implementation and its checks, then the JSDoc in `node_modules/@dylanebert/shallot/src/` for the APIs it uses.
- Check your work as that example's checks do, with the cheapest evidence that answers: state, then a captured frame, then the browser.
- While you iterate, run only the check that answers your change: `bun test ./<file>` or `bunx playwright test <file>`. Before you finish, run `bun check` and `bun test` once; CI, `.github/workflows/test.yml`, runs every tier.
- `bun test` runs `*.test.ts` and `*.gpu.test.ts` only; run a `*.node.ts` check by path with `bun test ./<file>`. A full renderer or physics composition is a `tests/<goal>.node.ts` check, not a `*.gpu.test.ts`.
- `bunx shallot publish` builds, publishes to Cloudflare, or to itch.io with `--target itch`, and verifies the public game; read `bunx shallot publish --help` first. Commit its `package.json` destination and dependency changes. A first-link name collision refuses rather than overwrites; do not write `shallot.publish` by hand unless updating that Worker is explicitly intended. An itch.io page is created and set up by a person on itch.io; publish names the settings it cannot verify. A processed itch.io build awaiting a page view succeeds without interaction but is reported unverified; open the named page, then publish again to verify it.
- Cleanup, rollback and listing stay the provider's; `bunx shallot publish --help` names each command from the project's link. Confirm with the person before deleting a Worker or taking a page down: Wrangler's delete asks nothing without a TTY or in CI.
- Publishing without interaction needs the provider's credentials (`CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, plus `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` when ambiguous; butler's stored credentials or `BUTLER_API_KEY` for itch.io). CI's least Cloudflare token is custom, with Account → Workers Scripts → Edit on the one account; the "Edit Cloudflare Workers" template is broader. butler's login key has `wharf` scope, managing builds on every project the identity can reach, not one game; an account-settings API key can be broader still. Never put credentials in `package.json`. Publish adds no credentials to the build; Vite's client values, public files and source maps can still disclose what the project puts there. Never put secrets in them.

</project_instructions>
</project_context>

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

Show a cube that starts out white. When I press the spacebar, it should turn green and stay green.
Before I press anything it should be white, and the change should happen the moment I hit space.

Keep it simple — one cube, keyboard only.

I replaced the spinning welcome scene with a single cube that starts white and turns green when you press Space. It stays green after that. The type check, unit tests and browser tests all pass, including a browser run with a real Space press.

**What's in the scene:** one cube, a light and a fixed camera. I removed the ground and the mouse-driven orbit camera, so the only control is the keyboard.

**How it works** (`src/cube/index.ts`): every frame, a small system checks whether Space was pressed. The first time it is, it changes the cube's color to green and remembers that it did, so later presses do nothing. The check runs at the start of each frame, so the frame where you press Space is already drawn green. Other keys leave the cube white.

**Files:**
- `index.html`: now loads the cube scene instead of the welcome one, with an updated page description.
- `src/welcome/`: deleted.

**Checks:**
- `src/cube/cube.test.ts`: the cube starts white and stays white with no input or other keys; Space turns it green on that same frame; it stays green after you let go and after pressing Space again.
- `tests/cube.e2e.ts`: in a real browser, the middle of the screen shows white until Space is pressed, then green, and it stays green.

You can try it with `bun run dev`.
